newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Queensland positive on Century talks.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Queensland positive on Century talks.

text.p: The Queensland state government said on Thursday it was confident talks between former Australian governor-general Bill Hayden and Aboriginal groups next week will see a resolution to land rights disputes delaying RTZ Plc-CRA Ltd's A$1 billion Century zinc mine.
"It is our view that the six-month opening period of negotiations will end on February 13. We think we could get a result before than," a spokesman for Queensland premier Rob Borbidge told Reuters.
Talks between Century Zinc and Aboriginal groups in far north Queensland started on August 16 with Hayden appointed by the state government earlier this month to facilitate negotiations.
Hayden is scheduled to visit several areas next week to start talks with Aboriginal groups.
Negotiations under the Native Title Act were expected to last six months, with a further six-month arbitration process allowed if agreement was not reached in the first stage.
"The indications are that the (Aboriginal) claimants will form into two groups, instead of the current five," Borbidge's spokesman said.
One of the two groups were likely to be members of the Waanyi tribe, on whose land the Century mine is to be built, the spokesman said.
The other group were non-Waanyi people whose land claims were along the proposed slurry pipeline running to the Gulf of Carpentaria, he said.
Century Zinc's general manager, public affairs, Jim Singer said the company's position regarding the current talks remained unchanged.
"We are hopeful of a successful outcome during the negotiating period," Singer said.
Century has already warned that the longer the negotiating process takes, the less the chance of supplying Century's zinc output to the Netherland's Budel smelter.
Pasminco Ltd was to be Century's biggest customer, purchasing half of the projected 780,000 tonnes of low iron-bearing zinc concentrate annually for the Budel smelter.
Century's development is crucial to the continued operations of Budel, whose current licence requires it to halt the production of jarosite, a zinc process residue, by June 1998.
